chunks.title: What Python is — running a program, input and output
chunks.content: Python is an interpreted programming language with short, readable syntax. Python uses indentation to create code blocks instead of curly braces: the lines that belong to the body of an if, for, while or a function must be indented to the same level. The print() function displays data on the screen; the input() function reads data that the user types on the keyboard and always returns a string (str). A comment line starts with the # symbol, and Python ignores it when running the program.

chunks.title: Basic data types, operators and type conversion
chunks.content: The basic data types are int (integers, e.g. 5), float (real numbers, e.g. 3.14), str (strings, e.g. 'hello') and bool (True / False). Convert between types with int('5'), float('2.5') and str(10). Operators: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division which always gives a float (7 / 2 = 3.5), // floor division which keeps only the integer part (7 // 2 = 3), % remainder (7 % 2 = 1) and ** power (2 ** 3 = 8). Adding a string to a number (e.g. '5' + 1) raises a TypeError, so you must convert the type first.

chunks.title: Lists and tuples
chunks.content: A list is written in square brackets, e.g. [1, 2, 3], and is mutable: you can add an item with append(), change an item with a[0] = 9, and remove an item with remove() or del. A tuple is written in parentheses, e.g. (1, 2, 3), and is immutable: it cannot be changed after it is created. Use a tuple for fixed data such as coordinates (x, y) or dates (day, month, year); a tuple can also be used as a dictionary key, a list cannot. Both are indexed from 0, and len() returns the number of items.

chunks.title: Algorithms and programs
chunks.content: An algorithm is a finite sequence of clear steps, in a defined order, that solves a problem by turning the input into the output. Properties of an algorithm: finiteness (it must stop after a number of steps), definiteness (each step is clear and has only one meaning), and it has input and output. A program is an algorithm written in a programming language so that a computer can carry it out.

chunks.title: The three basic control structures and flowcharts
chunks.content: Every algorithm is built from three basic control structures: sequence (steps are done one after another), selection or branching (do one thing or another depending on a condition) and iteration or repetition (do something many times). A flowchart shows an algorithm as a drawing: an oval is start / end, a rectangle is a processing step, a parallelogram is input / output, a diamond is a branching condition, and arrows show the direction of flow.

chunks.title: Types of errors and debugging
chunks.content: There are three common types of errors. A syntax error (SyntaxError) breaks the rules of the language, e.g. a missing colon after if, so the program cannot run. A runtime error stops the program while it is running, e.g. dividing by 0 raises ZeroDivisionError and using a variable that was never assigned raises NameError. A logic error lets the program run normally without any error message, but the result is wrong, e.g. because of a wrong condition. Debugging means finding the mistake by printing the values of variables or running the program step by step.

chunks.title: The for loop and range()
chunks.content: A for loop visits each item of a sequence (a list, a string, a range) one by one. range(n) produces the numbers 0, 1, ..., n-1 (n is not included). range(a, b) produces numbers from a to b-1. range(a, b, step) starts at a, increases by step each time and stops before b; e.g. range(2, 10, 3) gives 2, 5, 8. Use for when the number of repetitions is known in advance or when you need to go through each item of a list.

chunks.title: The while loop
chunks.content: A while loop repeats its block of code as long as the condition is true and stops when the condition becomes false. The body of the loop must update the variable used in the condition (e.g. i += 1); otherwise the condition stays true forever and the program loops infinitely. Use while when the number of repetitions is not known in advance, e.g. asking for a password until the user enters the correct one, or reading data until a stop value appears.

chunks.title: break, continue and accumulator variables
chunks.content: The break statement exits the loop completely, so the remaining iterations do not run. The continue statement skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next iteration. An accumulator variable is used to count or to add up values: initialise it before the loop (e.g. total = 0, count = 0) and add to it inside the loop body (total += i). Example of adding 1 to n: n = int(input()); total = 0; for i in range(1, n + 1): total += i.

chunks.title: Variables and assignment
chunks.content: A variable is a name attached to a value stored in memory, used to store data and use it again. Assignment uses the = sign, e.g. x = 5 means assigning the value 5 to the variable x (= is not a comparison). Assigning again changes the value of the variable: x = x + 1, or the short form x += 1, increases x by 1. Python can assign several variables at once and swap them quickly: a, b = b, a.

chunks.title: Rules for naming variables
chunks.content: A variable name in Python must start with a letter or an underscore (_), cannot start with a digit, cannot contain spaces or special characters (such as -, @, #), and cannot be a Python keyword (if, for, while, class, def...). Variable names are case-sensitive: Total and total are two different variables. Convention: use meaningful names in lowercase joined by underscores (snake_case), e.g. total_score. Valid examples: total_sum, _count, x1; invalid: 2nums, total sum, for.

chunks.title: Dynamic typing
chunks.content: Python is a dynamically typed language: you do not declare a type when you create a variable, and Python works out the type from the value assigned while the program runs. The same variable can later be assigned a value of another type, e.g. x = 10 (int) and then x = 'ten' (str). The type(x) function returns the current type of a variable. None is a special value meaning 'no value' (e.g. x = None). This is different from a variable that was never assigned: using an unassigned variable raises NameError.

chunks.title: The if, elif and else statements
chunks.content: The if statement checks a condition: if it is true, the indented block below it runs. elif (short for else if) checks another condition when all the previous conditions are false. else runs when all the conditions above are false. In an if / elif / else chain exactly one branch runs: the first branch whose condition is true. A colon (:) must follow the condition and the block must be indented.

chunks.title: Comparison operators and logical operators
chunks.content: Comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, >=; the result is True or False. Note: == compares, = assigns. Logical operators: and is true when both sides are true; or is true when at least one side is true; not reverses the value. Examples: True and False gives False, True or False gives True, not True gives False. String comparison is case-sensitive.

chunks.title: Nested conditions, branch order and falsy values
chunks.content: An if can be placed inside another if (nested conditions). The order of elif branches matters: because only the first true branch runs, a broad condition placed first will block the branches after it. For example, grading a score must go from high to low: if score >= 8 (Excellent), elif score >= 6.5 (Good), elif score >= 5 (Average), else (Weak). In a condition, the values 0, the empty string '', the empty list [] and None are treated as False (falsy); all other values are treated as True.

rubric.text: / is normal division and the result is always a real number (float)
// is floor division (keeps only the integer part)

Use len() to get the number of items

questions.content: The user enters two integers on the keyboard. Write (or describe) a program that prints their sum, and explain why you have to convert the input.

Convert it to a number with int() (or float())
Print the sum with print()
Explanation: input() returns a string, and adding two strings only joins them (e.g. '5' + '3' = '53')

questions.explanation: Model answer: a = int(input()) and b = int(input()) read two numbers and convert them to integers. Then print(a + b) prints the sum. We must convert them because input() always returns a string, so without converting, '5' + '3' would be joined into '53'.

It must use as little memory as possible
It must stop after a finite number of steps

questions.content: What is a common way to find where a logic error is?

Turn the computer off and run again
Print the values of variables to check them

questions.content: Name the three basic control structures used to build algorithms and briefly explain each one.

rubric.text: Sequence: the steps are done one after another
Selection (branching): do one thing or another depending on a condition
Iteration: do something many times

questions.explanation: Model answer: Sequence means the steps are done one after another from top to bottom. Selection (branching) means choosing to do one thing or another depending on a condition. Iteration means doing something many times.

questions.content: How is a syntax error different from a logic error? Give an example of each.

rubric.text: A syntax error breaks the rules of the language, so the program cannot run
A logic error: the program still runs without an error message, but the result is wrong
A sensible example (a missing colon; a wrong condition...)

questions.explanation: Model answer: A syntax error breaks the rules of the language, so the program cannot run, for example a missing colon after if. A logic error means the program still runs without any error message but the result is wrong, for example a wrong condition.

questions.content: Write an algorithm (as steps) that finds the larger of two numbers a and b. State the input, the output and the control structure used.

rubric.text: Input: enter the two numbers a, b
Compare a with b (e.g. if a > b take a, otherwise take b)
Output: print the larger number
Selection structure (if / else)

questions.explanation: Model answer: Step 1: enter the two numbers a and b, this is the input. Step 2: compare a with b; if a > b then max = a, otherwise max = b. Step 3: print max, this is the output. The algorithm uses a selection structure because it has to choose based on a condition.

questions.content:
This program should compute the average of two numbers, but it prints a wrong result:
a = 4
b = 6
avg = a + b / 2
print(avg)
What type of error is this, why is it wrong, how do you fix it, and name one way to debug it.

rubric.text: It is a logic error
Why it is wrong: the division is done before the addition (it prints 7.0)
Fix: add parentheses, avg = (a + b) / 2
Debugging: print the values of the variables or run step by step

questions.explanation: Model answer: This is a logic error because the program still runs but prints 7.0 instead of 5. The cause is that division has a higher priority and is done before addition, so only b is divided by 2. Fix it as avg = (a + b) / 2 so that the addition is done first and then the division. To debug it, you can print the value of each variable or run the program step by step.

questions.content: Describe in words (or as a flowchart) an algorithm that checks whether an integer n is even or odd. State which flowchart shape is used for the input step, the condition check and the start / end.

rubric.text: Input n uses a parallelogram
Even condition: n % 2 == 0 (divisible by 2)
The condition is placed in a diamond
Two branches: if true print even, if false print odd
Start / end uses an oval

questions.explanation: Model answer: Start with an oval. Input the number n in a parallelogram. Check the condition n % 2 == 0 in a diamond. If it is true, print that the number is even, otherwise print that the number is odd. Finally, end with an oval.

questions.content: When should you use a for loop, and when should you use a while loop?

rubric.text: for: when the number of repetitions is known in advance, or to go through each item of a sequence
while: when the number of repetitions is not known in advance; it repeats based on a condition

questions.content: Write (or describe) a program that uses a loop to add up the numbers from 1 to n, where n is entered on the keyboard. Explain each part.

rubric.text: Read n and convert it to an integer with int(input())
Initialise the sum variable to 0 before the loop
The loop runs from 1 to n, e.g. range(1, n + 1)
Add each number to the sum (total += i)

questions.explanation: Model answer: n = int(input()) converts the input to a number; total = 0 initialises the sum variable; for i in range(1, n + 1) runs i from 1 to n; total += i adds each number to the total; finally print(total).

It runs the current iteration again

questions.content: Which loop is suitable when the number of repetitions is NOT known in advance?

questions.content: Explain the meaning of the three parameters of range(a, b, step), and say which numbers range(1, 10, 4) produces.

The sequence stops before b (b is not included)

questions.content: Write (or describe) a program that asks the user to enter a password until they enter 'abc123', and then prints 'Login successful'. Explain why you use while instead of for.

rubric.text: while with the condition that the password is still wrong (pw != 'abc123')
Enter the password again with input() inside the loop body
Print the message with print() once it is correct (after the loop)
Explanation: we do not know in advance how many times the user will try

questions.explanation: Model answer: First pw = input() reads the password the first time. Use while pw != 'abc123' to repeat while the password is still wrong. Inside the loop body call pw = input() to enter it again. When the loop ends, print('Login successful'). Use while because we do not know in advance how many times the user will try.

questions.content: Write (or describe) a program that counts how many even numbers are in the list nums = [3, 8, 5, 10, 6]. Explain the role of the counter variable.

rubric.text: Initialise the counter to 0 before the loop
Go through each item with for
Even-number condition: x % 2 == 0

questions.explanation: Model answer: Initialise count = 0 before the loop so that counting starts from zero. Use for x in nums to go through each item. For each item, if x % 2 == 0 then it is an even number. When an even number is found, count += 1 increases the counter. The result is count = 3 because of 8, 10 and 6.
